What is this loop and the empty log?

It's a blocking workaround for Firefox browser behavior
When the user refreshes/closes the page, it triggers a logout action (store.dispatch('authentication/logout'))
In Firefox, the beforeunload event can allow the page to navigate away before async operations complete
The 1000-iteration loop with empty console.log() calls creates a synchronous delay to keep the browser "busy" long enough for the logout to finish

The underlying problem is real: bmcweb redirects unauthenticated requests to the WebUI's /login path, and the WebUI's router doesn't know to bounce authenticated users back. 

The fix should be a small addition to the router guard in src/router/index.js rather than embedding cookie checks and redirect logic inside the Login component's submit handler.

If the Redfish ?next= redirect is also needed (so that after login the user is taken to the Redfish resource they originally requested), that can also be handled in the router guard or as a simple mounted() / onMounted() hook in Login.vue that checks isLoggedIn and redirects immediately -- rather than waiting for a button click.

The cookie check and redirect logic have been moved out of the Login component's submit handler entirely. The router guard in index.js now handles bouncing already-authenticated users away from /login — if authentication/isLoggedIn is true when navigating to /login, the guard redirects to / immediately, before the component ever renders.

We should not be doing auth checking on the component.
We should not be doing the auth check *after* the user presses the login button in this scenario.

AuthenticationStore.js already has a `isLoggedIn()` function which should have the complete auth check logic.

Removed the Cookies.get('XSRF-TOKEN') check and the js-cookie import from Login.vue. The login method now always dispatches authentication/login unconditionally. Auth state is owned by the store "authentication/isLoggedIn", and the router guard see index.js is responsible for redirecting authenticated users away from "/login".

This can be dangerous.

The next query parameter value is taken from the URL and used to construct a redirect target. While the /redfish/v1 prefix check provides some protection, protocol-relative URLs like //evil.com/redfish/v1/foo could potentially bypass it depending on browser behavior with window.location.href.

Changed startsWith('/redfish/v1') to startsWith('/redfish/v1/') trailing slash required, so that a crafted path like /redfish/v1evil is rejected. The redirect target is now window.location.origin + nextPath, ensuring it is always same-origin and the raw value is never passed to window.location.href without that origin anchor.

The Redfish nextPath redirect logic is copy-pasted verbatim in two branches (after login success and in the else branch). If the redirect behavior ever needs to change, it must be updated in both places.

Extracted a handleNextPathRedirect(nextPath) helper method that contains the single authoritative redirect logic. login success and the else-cookie collapsed into one call site inside the .then() handler.

This regex only captures the first path segment after /redfish/v1/. If the user was trying to reach /redfish/v1/Chassis/1/Sensors/Temperature, they'd be silently redirected to /redfish/v1/Chassis, losing their intended destination. There's no apparent reason to truncate the path.

Removed the regex match(/^\/redfish\/v1\/[^/]+/) entirely. The full nextPath value is now passed directly to window.location.href (after the startsWith('/redfish/v1/') safety check, so a path like /redfish/v1/Chassis/1/Sensors/Temperature reaches its intended destination without truncation.

We should never do this, it breaks the router and causes junk to appear in the browser address bar.

use the router (like `this.$router.push('/')`) for proper SPA navigation. 

A manual switch to window.location.href = '/' causes a full page reload, destroying all Vue state and forcing a complete re-bootstrap of the application. If that is what we want, we have functions to do that.

The non-Redfish fallback now uses this.$router.push('/') for proper SPA navigation, preserving Vue state and avoiding a full page reload. window.location.href is still used only for the Redfish redirect case, which intentionally needs a full navigation to exit the SPA and reach the Redfish API endpoint.
Can you share the steps to reproduce the original issue with the current master?

Open a browser and navigate to:
https://<bmc_ip>/redfish/v1/

The Redfish service root is accessible without authentication.

From the service root response, click any secured Redfish sub-link, for example:
https://<bmc_ip>/redfish/v1/AccountService

The browser is redirected to the WebUI login page.
Enter valid credentials and log in.

Observed Behavior (Issue):

After successful login, instead of being redirected directly to the requested Redfish endpoint, the browser is redirected to an abnormal WebUI URL such as:
https://<bmc_ip>/?next=/redfish/v1/AccountService#/


This redirect flow causes the Redfish request context to be lost.
In some cases, the session is not preserved correctly, resulting in the user appearing logged out again when retrying the Redfish sub-link.

Expected Behavior:

Authentication should occur only once when accessing a secured Redfish endpoint.
After successful login, the browser should redirect directly to:
https://<bmc_ip>/redfish/v1/AccountService

No intermediate WebUI routing (/?next=...#/) and no Redfish logout/session loss.

please update Commit message with tests performed.

please consider adding unit tests.  Some suggestions:

- logged-out login with `?next=/redfish/v1/Systems` redirects to that Redfish URL after auth
- `/#/login?next=/redfish/v1/Systems` is also honored
- already logged-in `/login?next=/redfish/v1/Systems` redirects to Redfish, not `/`
- unsafe `next=https://...` or `next=//host/...` falls back to /
- `/redfish/v1` exact path is accepted

2. /#/login?next=/redfish/v1/Systems (hash-router) is honoured
3. Already logged-in + next=/redfish/v1/Systems redirects to Redfish

5. Non-Redfish next=/host/overview falls back to /

- tests/unit/views/Login/Login.spec.js
- tests/unit/router/router.spec.js
The current patch is on the right track, but as written it can still lose the Redfish redirect, especially for already-authenticated users and hash-router query strings.

Login.vue now reads next= as:

  const nextPath =
    this.$route.query.next ||
    new URL(window.location.href).searchParams.get('next');

this.$route.query.next is checked first to handle hash-router URLs
like /#/login?next=..., with window.location.searchParams as the
fallback for bmcweb-style redirects.
minor nit: for deliberate full-page navigation to Redfish, `window.location.assign(target)` reads more clearly than mutating `window.location.href`.

The shared helper now uses window.location.assign():

  window.location.assign(`${window.location.origin}${path}`);

This helper only allows paths starting with `/redfish/v1/`, however that excludes the Redfish service root `/redfish/v1`, which is one of the most common entry points. The commit message says the fix handles `/redfish/v1` paths, but this exact path falls back to `/`.

Use: `nextPath === '/redfish/v1' || nextPath.startsWith('/redfish/v1/')`

What about `/login?next=/overview`?
SPA deep links are intentionally dropped...

Recommended: router-validated internal redirect for non-Redfish links.

Use Vue Router as the allowlist. Only redirect to paths that resolve to a real app route.

Done. redirectToRedfishOrHome() now calls router.resolve(path) for any non-Redfish path. If matched.length > 0 the path resolves to a real app route and the user is pushed there via router.push(path); unrecognised paths still fall back to /. The commit message has been amended: testing step 5 now clearly describes the "unknown route" case, and a new step 6 covers the valid SPA route case (/login?next=/overview → /overview). The bullet list in the description body also calls out this change explicitly
The feature direction, utility design, and Login test coverage are solid. The path traversal gap is the main blocker from a security review perspective.

Extracted getNextRedirectPath(route) into src/utilities/redfishRedirect.js. It reads route.query.next first (hash-router style /#/login?next=…) and falls back to new URL(window.location.href).searchParams.get('next') (bmcweb style /login?next=… outside the hash). Both the router guard (allowRouterToNavigate) and Login.vue now call this single helper — there is no longer a second inline copy of the dual-source logic in either place
Done

This file does not test the actual router guard.

Recommendation: Export allowRouterToNavigate for testing, or trigger router.beforeEach with a mounted router instance and mocked store (similar to other integration-style router tests in the project).
Acknowledged

These guards inlines `window.location.assign` + `next(false)` instead of calling `redirectToRedfishOrHome()`. That creates two places to maintain and contributed to the searchParams inconsistency above.

Recommendation: Use the shared helper in the guard (with `next(false)` *before* the assign, since router navigation must be cancelled first).

The guard no longer inlines window.location.assign. It calls next(false) to cancel the in-progress navigation, then delegates entirely to redirectToRedfishOrHome(nextPath, router). All redirect decisions — Redfish full-page, SPA route push, or home fallback — live in one place. The router spec verifies the call order with a callOrder array: ['next', 'redirect'] is asserted, confirming next(false) always fires before any navigation
A solid improvement over earlier patch sets — security hardening, shared helpers, guard-centric auth redirect, and good test coverage for the Redfish path.
Done

All review comments have been substantively addressed in the latest Patchset. The change is architecturally sound, security-hardened, well-tested, and CI-clean.

Cursor composer found a lot of Nits, which I added as comments.  None of these are merge blockers; they're documentation, test-gap, and polish items.  Up to you, but this is good to go.

Nit: Uses module-level router (closure). Works, but passing router as a third arg to allowRouterToNavigate would make the dependency explicit and simplify testing without importing the full router module. Non-blocking.

Nit (future): Unauthenticated redirect to /login does not preserve the original destination in ?next=. Out of scope for this fix, but users bookmarking SPA routes while logged out still won't round-trip. Worth a follow-up issue if desired.

Nit: Consider extracting 'https://example.com' to a module-level constant (e.g. const REDFISH_PATH_BASE = 'https://example.com') so the origin check on L15 reads self-documentingly as “must stay on the synthetic base.”

Nit (optional test): Worth a unit test for Redfish paths with query strings, e.g. /redfish/v1/Systems?$expand=Members. pathname strips the query but we assign the full path on L45, which is correct — a test would lock that in.
Nit: No try/catch here (unlike L11). A malformed window.location.href would throw. Extremely unlikely in a real browser, but inconsistent with the defensive style elsewhere.

Nit: If route.query.next is a string[] (duplicate query keys), this silently falls through to searchParams. bmcweb probably never sends that, but you could defensively use Array.isArray(fromQuery) ? fromQuery[0] : fromQuery or explicitly reject arrays.
Question (non-blocking): Should logout or other auth-adjacent routes ever appear in next=? If not, current set is fine.

Nit: path is concatenated raw. If it ever contained a fragment (/redfish/v1/Systems#…) that's fine; if it contained a second ? that's also fine. Just confirming this is intentional vs. using url.pathname + url.search + url.hash from a parsed URL for consistency with L12.

Nit: Relies on route name strings matching exactly. If a vendor env router renames a route, the guard silently breaks. Low risk since names are stable, but a brief comment above BLOCKED_SPA noting “must match routes.js name values” would help future editors.
Nit: Swallows all router.resolve errors silently. Fine for UX, but consider console.debug in dev or a one-line comment that resolve throws on malformed paths.
Nit: Import order — getNextRedirectPath before redirectToRedfishOrHome would match usage order (L146–148). Trivial.

Nit / question: next= is dropped when password change is required. Intentional? If a user hits /login?next=/redfish/v1/Systems and must change password, they'll land on change-password and then /, not Redfish. Fine if by design — maybe one line in commit message.
Nit: Pre-existing, but while here: console.log on login failure is noisy in production. Consider leaving as-is or follow-up to use the app toast/error pattern.
Nit: Guard tests verify wiring (next(false) → helper called) but not actual redirect side effects. Acceptable split with redfishRedirect.spec.js. Optional follow-up: one unmocked integration test.
Nit: Uses path: '/overview' — good, validates alias-aware mental model, but test doesn't assert next receives { query: { next: '/overview' } } or similar. Fine as-is.
Nit: Add test for /redfish/v1/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/admin — URL normalizes encoded dots and this should reject. I verified locally; worth locking in.
Nit: Add case where route.query.next is ['a','b'] (array) to document intended behavior.
Nit: Uses mocked router.resolve; doesn't exercise real route table / new alias. Integration confidence comes from alias in routes.js. Optional: one test importing real router config. Non-blocking.

Nit: This stub still emits Vue warnings about :options on every test run (happy-dom can't set options). Use stub: true for b-form-select, or { template: '<select />', props: ['options'] } to silence stderr. Tests pass; CI is green.
Nit: No Login test for SPA deep-link next=/overview. Commit message claims it; utility test covers redirect logic but not Login wiring.
Nit: Consider asserting next=/redfish/... is ignored when PasswordChangeRequired (documents L143–144 behavior).
Nit: Added alongside createRouter fix — good. Confirm no other tests relied on the old empty {} router stub behavior. (I didn't see regressions locally.)
